metrics.label: Henry Hub gas

metrics.label: Coal API2 (ARA)

metrics.label: Heating oil / gasoil

metrics.label: RBOB gasoline

metrics.label: Dry bulk ETF (BDRY)

metrics.label: Baltic Capesize Index
metrics.blurb: The Capesize component of the Baltic Dry Index. The most volatile part, and effectively a bet on Chinese steel production.

metrics.label: Baltic Panamax Index
metrics.blurb: The Panamax component. Coal and grain rather than iron ore, so it follows harvests and power demand more than steel.

metrics.label: Baltic Supramax Index
metrics.blurb: The Supramax component. These ships have their own cranes and serve smaller ports, so it reflects broad trade rather than one commodity.

metrics.label: Diesel crack vs Brent

brief.text:
The clearest move in today's data is in crude. Brent, the global benchmark grade of oil, fell 4.0% to $88.91 a barrel this afternoon, with WTI, its US equivalent, down 3.8% to $80.20. Nothing in today's headlines explains the drop, so the data here does not show why. For anyone fixing ships, cheaper crude cuts the cost of bunkers (ship fuel) over time, but it can also signal softer cargo demand; today the two are pointing in different directions, because freight sentiment firmed at the same time. The Baltic Dry Index, which measures the cost of moving bulk cargoes like iron ore, coal and grain, rose 102 points (+3.5%) to 3,000, confirmed by trade press reporting the same number.

On prices, refined products followed crude down: gasoil fell 4.7% to $3.74 a gallon and RBOB gasoline 3.0% to $2.43. US Henry Hub gas dropped 8.2% to $3.13/mmBtu, again unexplained by the data. Bunkers were mixed and mostly flat: VLSFO (very low sulphur fuel oil) was $842/t in Singapore, up 1.0%, but down 1.3% in Rotterdam to $705.50, with Fujairah $800.00 and Houston $720.50. Freight equities rose — the dry bulk ETF BDRY up 5.0% to $12.73, the tanker ETF BWET up 2.2% to $762.23. Most tanker earnings figures are a session old: VLCC TD3C (very large crude carrier, Arabian Gulf to China) stood at $1,079,794 a day on Sunday 22 November, Suezmax TD20 at $165,677 and MR TC2 at just $11,300. Today's LNG rates: BLNG1 Australia–Japan $50,600/day, BLNG3 US Gulf–Japan $40,400/day.

Running stories were largely quiet. Hormuz developed: a report that an Iranian tanker with no track record signalled it had passed a US blockade outside the strait underlines how unreliable vessel tracking has become there — relevant when verifying counterparties. The Baltic drone strike on the RoRo Sparta II, the Black Sea attacks, Russian refinery damage and diesel export limits, shadow-fleet sanctions and the US–China ship-fee suspension all had no news today and are unchanged.

Watch two things. First, whether the Capesize, Panamax and Supramax indices (the Baltic's size-by-size dry bulk gauges, last seen Friday 20 November at 4,502, 2,140 and 1,810) confirm today's BDI gain. Second, IMO working group ISWG-GHG 23, which opened today on the Net Zero Framework — future fuel and compliance costs.

storylines.title: Attacks and escalation around Hormuz
storylines.what: Attacks on commercial shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz continue, following tanker incidents near Oman, a mine strike east of Hormuz and a projectile hit on an outbound tanker. Tracking and identity obfuscation around the strait is now also in question.
storylines.why_it_matters: Hull strikes and mines raise war-risk premiums for Arabian Gulf liftings, slow transits and shrink the pool of willing owners, reshaping crude, product and gas ton-miles. Unreliable AIS signalling makes vessel vetting and position verification harder.
storylines.latest: An Iranian tanker with no track record signalled on Monday that it had sailed past a US blockade outside the Strait of Hormuz, raising questions about obfuscation tactics and the limits of traffic analysis.
sources: Fake Iran Tanker Highlights Uncertainty Around Hormuz Traffic

storylines.title: Drone strikes on shipping in the Baltic and Gulf of Finland
storylines.what: The Russian RoRo Sparta II, linked to military logistics, was struck by a suspected drone on Saturday while sailing in the Baltic, catching fire and drifting into Finnish territorial waters.
storylines.why_it_matters: Attacks in the Baltic extend the risk zone for merchant shipping well beyond the Black Sea, with implications for war-risk cover, routing and port calls in Northern Europe.

storylines.title: Attacks on shipping in the Black Sea
storylines.what: Drone strikes on merchant ships in the Black Sea have continued through November, with two vessels sunk off Bulgaria and crew injured following an earlier wheat carrier capsizing.
storylines.why_it_matters: Strikes on ships and port infrastructure threaten grain and dry bulk loadings and add insurance and routing costs for any vessel calling in the region.

storylines.title: Russian refining damage and diesel export limits
storylines.what: Ukrainian drone attacks have cut Russian refineries' combined crude processing by 45% since late October, on top of a Russian ban on most diesel exports extended to end-January.
storylines.why_it_matters: Lost Russian refining and export restrictions reshape clean product ton-miles, pulling diesel from longer-haul sources and changing MR and LR employment.

storylines.title: Sanctions and evasion in the shadow fleet
storylines.what: Sanctions pressure on the shadow fleet is widening, with EU measures targeting shipowners, managers, insurers and financial networks, adding to earlier US designations. The Russian Navy is reported escorting sanctioned dark-fleet tankers in the Mediterranean.
storylines.why_it_matters: Designations force charterers and underwriters to re-verify counterparties and vessel positions, and obfuscated signalling makes that verification harder.

storylines.title: US-China ship fees and port state control friction
storylines.what: The US has extended its suspension of port fees targeting Chinese-built and Chinese-operated vessels for another two months while trade talks continue, while a US congressional committee urges sanctions over China's detention of Panama-flagged ships.
storylines.why_it_matters: Reinstated fees, sanctions or retaliatory detentions would change the cost and risk of deploying particular tonnage into US and Chinese trades.
